newsitem.title: CANADA: Ontario Hydro launches massive nuclear overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Ontario Hydro launches massive nuclear overhaul.

text.p: Government-owned Ontario Hydro, North America's largest power utility, unveiled on Wednesday a multi-billion dollar overhaul of its troubled nuclear power operations, including a shutdown of seven nuclear units.

The massive effort will cost the debt-laden utility between C$5 billion ($3.6 billion) and C$8 billion ($5.7 billion), but will not force a hike in power rates for the utility's 3.8 million customers.
The shakeup followed a scathing report that criticized management and forced the resignation of President and Chief Executive Allan Kupcis on Tuesday.

The report commissioned by Kupcis found a "lack of authoritative and accountable managerial leadership" and concluded the performance of the five nuclear plants were "minimally acceptable" for a North American nuclear operation.
But it also stressed the public's safety was not at risk.
"Our problems are people, not machines," Ontario Hydro Chairman and interim Chief Executive William Farlinger told reporters on Wednesday.
"My own theory is that the nuclear unit was operated over the years as some sort of special nuclear cult," Farlinger said, adding that more resignations were likely.

Under the plan outlined on Wednesday, four nuclear units at the Pickering A station and three units at Bruce A station would be shut over the next year. A heavy water plant at Bruce will be permanently closed.
In addition, Ontario Hydro is considering writing off C$2 billion ($1.44 billion) in assets this year.
Ontario Hydro said it would replace the electricity generated by the laid up units by operating existing fossil-fuel plants at higher levels and bringing back mothballed units.
"This overhaul will not affect rates. We will uphold Hydro's current mandate to meet all the electricity supply needs of our customers," Farlinger said.
Extensive upgrades would also be made at the utility's Pickering B and Bruce B stations and Darlington plant. No major layoffs are planned.
The cost of the overhaul will not add to the utility's debt, but plans to cut debt by C$2 billion ($1.4 billion) a year over the next five years will be deferred.

Ontario Hydro is the continent's largest electricity producer based on installed generating capacity. It operates 69 hydro-electric stations, five nuclear stations and six fossil-fuel plants in Canada's industrial heartland.
The restructuring comes as the utility is struggling under C$33 billion ($24 billion) in debt and preparing for competition in Ontario's power market.

A report last year by a government-appointed committee recommended that the utility lose its 91-year-old monopoly and face competition or Ontario's 3.8 million customers ranging from households to heavy industry.

Earlier this year, Ontario's Conservative government backed away from its 1995 election promise to sell off the giant utility. But some analysts said the overhaul could make privatization a more attractive option in the future.
"I believe that one of the hindrances to privatization was that no on wanted the nuclear portion," said Sheldon Dong, manager of fixed-income research with Midland Walwyn Capital.
Major debt rating agencies confirmed their ratings on the province of Ontario and Ontario Hydro on Wednesday, but said the utility and province faced many challenges.

New York-based Standard & Poor's said the province could accommodate the financial impact of the restructuring, but it "has the potential to push back the overall improvement in the province's credit profile, notwithstanding the province's continuing progress with its own deficit."
